hints.content:
##Strategy

Let's first find the indefinite integral $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\,$.  Then we can use the result to compute the definite integral.

##Finding the indefinite integral

To find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\,$, we can use U-substitution.

If we let $\blueD {u=x^2+1}$, then ${du=2x \, dx}$ and $\maroonD{ x\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}\, du}$.  

So we have:


$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\,&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\blueD{x^2+1}}\,\cdot \maroonD{x\,dx}\,\,\\\\\\\\
&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{\blueD u}\,\cdot \maroonD{\dfrac12\, du}\,\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int\dfrac{1}{u}\,du\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|u|+C\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|x^2+1|+C\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+1)+C
\end{align}$

##Evaluating the definite integral

Now let's compute the definite integral:

$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int^{3}_{1}\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\,  &= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln(x^2+1)\Bigg|^3_1\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln(10)-\ln(2)\right)\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\ln(5)\end{align}$

[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
No, we could use U-substitution to calculate the definite integral directly. 

However, with this method, we must be sure to adjust our limits of integration.  

Here, when $\greenD{x=1}\,$, $\greenD{~u=2}~$ and when $~\goldD {x=3}\,$, $\goldD{u=10}\,$, so our limits of integration change respectively.

We can substitute to rewrite the definite integral as:

$\displaystyle\int^{\goldD 3}_{\greenD 1}\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx\, = \displaystyle\int^{\goldD {10}}_{\greenD 2}\dfrac{1}{ u}\,\cdot {\dfrac12\, du}\, $ 

We can now evaluate the definite integral as shown below:

$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int^{ {10}}_{ 2}\dfrac{1}{ u}\,\cdot {\dfrac12\, du}\,&=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int^{10}_{2}\dfrac{1}{u}\, du\, \\
\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\ln|u|\Bigg|^{10}_2\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\Big(\ln(10)-\ln(2)\Big) \\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\ln(5)
\end{align}$
